Public benches may seem like a small part of a city, but choices about where they are placed and how they are designed can raise bigger questions about public space. This story looks at research, personal experiences, and some widely discussed examples. As you listen, ask what does the evidence really show and what is still uncertain?
As he listened, notice why public benches matter to older adults.
As you listen, notice why public benches matter to older adults.
We have heard that benches give older adults a place to rest and spend time with others. But what happens when a bench is designed to limit how people can use it?

A public bench can be more than a place to sit. It can support rest and time with neighbors, but some designs can limit how it is used. The next two points will look at how to understand the evidence and check the examples in this debate.

So these two points remind us to be careful about what the evidence shows. The study describes people's experiences, and the famous bench cases need careful checking. Now let's hear how the article brings these ideas together.
Lived experience, not a final verdict.
Famous cases need careful checking.

A public bench is easy to ignore until you need one. For older adults, a place to sit can shape how they experience a neighborhood. A study in three nearby Vancouver neighborhoods interviewed adults aged 60 and older. They said benches gave them places to rest during walks. Benches also helps them enjoy green areas and waterfront spaces. But the role of a bench did not end there. The study described how benches can become like porches. They.Are neither fully private nor fully social. They create a simple place where neighbors can stop, talk or just spend time near one another. A 2023 review added a wider view. It examined 28 articles published from 2020 to 2023. The review reported that older park users preferred more benches linked to their desire to relax. Other literature in the review said that well-kempt parks with seating, pleasant paths, toilets and cafes.Encouraged older visitors.

At the same time, some public benches have been changed to limit how people use them. Sloped seats and center armrests can prevent people from lying across a bench. In other cases, benches are removed completely. These choices are often discussed as hostile architecture or defensive architecture. This creates a difficult question. Is a bench only a seat, or is it part of someone's ability to move through the city?A design that blocks one activity.May also remove a resting place for someone else. Yet the evidence about the wider harm remains limited. As of March 2021, article reported that no wide scale empirical study had measured the effects of hostile architecture on homeless people or other targeted groups.

The Vancouver researchers used seated interviews and walk along interviews at 2 times. There were 28 participants in 2012 and 22 in 2014. Their accounts show how people experienced their neighborhoods. They do not prove that adding benches will create the same results in every city.

公共のベンチ、なぜ今見直されているのか？
街にあるベンチは、ただの椅子なのでしょうか。今回のニュースは、公共のベンチと街の使いやすさについて考えます。ベンチの形やどこに置くかをめぐっては様々な意見があります。研究や実際の例を聞くと、公共の場所を誰がどのように使えるのかが見えてきます。聞き終える頃には、なぜベンチが街のあり方を考える手がかりになるのかがわかります。
高齢者にとってベンチがどんな役割を持つのかに注目して聞いてください。
ベンチは高齢の人が歩く途中で休む助けになります。では、そのベンチが使いにくくなったり、なくなったりすると、何が問題になるのでしょうか。
このニュースはベンチが休む場所であるだけでなく、人とのつながりや誰がその場所にいられるかにも関係することを伝えています。では、知らない人同士が使うベンチは、なぜ家のポーチのように考えられるのでしょうか。さらに、ベンチの形だけではわからないことにも注目して聞いてみましょう。
ここまで公共の場所で生まれる小さな交流と、ベンチの形だけでなく、実際の使われ方を確かめることについて聞きました。では、記事全体のまとめを英語で聞いてみましょう。
A porch shared by strangers.
The shape is not the whole story.

A bench does not move, but it can help a person keep moving. For an older adult, a long walk can become several shorter steps. There is time to stop, sit and rest before walking again. A study in three neighboring areas of Vancouver listened to adults aged 60 and older. Researchers used seated interviews and walk along talks. They met 28 participants in 2012 and 22 in 2014. The.Adults said benches helped them enjoy green spaces and places by the water. The seats gave them rest during walks. They also supported short talks and a feeling of connection. The researchers described this with a warm image. Benches become like porches. A porch is between private life and public life. A neighborhood bench can play a similar role. A 2023 review gives a wider view. It studied 28 articles published from 2020.To 2023, the review reported that older park users preferred more benches.Linked to their wish to relax.

Parks with seating, pleasant paths, toilets, cafes and good care were also reported to encourage older visitors. But public space can move in the opposite direction. Some benches are tilted or divided by middle armrests. Other benches are removed. When such changes are used to stop sleeping or other activities, they're called hostile architecture or defensive design. In 2021, an NYC transit social media.Post said subway benches were being removed to stop homeless people from sleeping on them. The post was later deleted. The MTA said it had been posted in error. It was not proof of an official removal policy. So the bench debate is not only about St. furniture, it is about who can rest, who can stay and how easily older adults can move through their community.

Many services use subscriptions, so the way they are designed matters. This story looks at what happens when people decide they no longer want one. Why has ending a subscription become an important consumer issue? By the end, you will understand the main debate behind that question.
As you listen, notice what can make canceling a subscription harder than starting one.

This story shows the gap between easy sign up and difficult cancellation. Next we will look at the different forms this difficulty can take and why a cancel button is not the whole issue.

So cancellation trouble can take many forms, and the cancel button is only one part of the process. The FTC Rule also focused on clear terms and real consent. Now let's hear how the article brings these ideas together.
Friction has many forms.
A cancel button is only part of the contract.

Starting a subscription often feels like an open door. One click and you are inside. Leaving can feel very different. The path may include extra screens, a phone call, or messages asking you to stay. This gap has a name, Sludge. Richard H Thaler discussed the idea in his 2018 science article Nudge, Not Sludge. A nudge helps people make a useful choice.Sludge adds friction when people try to do what they already want to do.For someone who no longer wants a subscription, that friction may stand between cancel and cancelled. A 2025 paper for the European Association of Cognitive Ergonomics annual conference examined dark patterns in subscription cancellation. This study used a review and a user experiment. It also analyzed 6 services as case examples. The Economist. Bloomberg, Scribd. Adobe Creative Cloud. Amazon Prime.And Audible.

The issue also reached US regulators. On October 16, 2024, the Federal Trade Commission finalized its click-to-cancel rule. It covered automatic renewals, free trials that become paid plans, and continuing product deliveries. Its central idea was simple. Leaving should be about as easy as joining. Cancellation should also be available through the same kind of channel used to sign up.The FTC had received more than 16,000 public comments since its March 2023 proposal. But the story did not end there. On July 8th, 2025, the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals vacated the whole rule for procedural reasons. After that decision, FTC guidance said the narrower negative option rule from the 1973 era returned. The broad Click to cancel standard was finalized, but it is not now.Force.

The 2025 study first identified 58 dark patterns in academic and Gray literature. It then standardized them into 44 patterns across 10 categories. These included complexity, misleading interfaces, forced continuation, retention efforts, and mental overload. Cancellation trouble is not just one annoying button.

The FTC rule went beyond the final click. It also called for clear key terms before billing, separate and sufficient consent, no false statements about important facts, and consent records kept for at least three years. An easy exit was part of a wider plan for informed agreement.
A subscription can begin with a tap, yet end in a maze. The debate over Sludge asks a plain question. If joining is easy, why should leaving be hard?

The real cost is the whole journey.
Researchers mapped the exit maze.

Starting a subscription can feel like walking through an open door. A free trial appears. The price is clear. A few clicks later, the service is running. Then you try to leave. The door is no longer easy to find. There may be more pages, confusing choices, requests to stay, or even a phone call. No single step looks huge. Together, however, they can make the exit feel heavy.This kind of friction has a name, sludge in choice design.Sludge means barriers that make it harder for people to do what they want or what helps them. For a customer who no longer wants a subscription, a difficult exit can fit this idea. Researchers also study these screens as dark patterns. the US Federal Trade Commission tried to change this structure.

Today's topic is growth now, profit later, when the startup race makes sense.

Some startups spend heavily and delay profit so they can grow quickly. This creates a difficult choice between speed and financial discipline. Understanding this issue can help you judge startup strategies more carefully. As you listen, ask under what conditions can growth before profit be a reasonable strategy?
Listen for why gaining users early can matter for some startups.
A network effect can make early growth valuable because each new user can make the product more useful. But how can we tell if fast growth is building a strong network or hiding a weak business?

The key message is that fast growth is not always a sign of strength. It can support a business with real network effects, but it can also hide serious weakness. The next two points will help us think about how to tell the difference.

So speed alone is not enough. Companies also need to track whether growth is efficient. At the same time, the market is showing more interest in efficiency and asking harder questions about rapid growth. Now let's hear the main take away.
Speed needs a dashboard.
The market is asking harder questions.

For some startups, profit is not the first finish line. They spend heavily to gain users, enter markets and grow faster than competitors. This can look dangerous, but when a company has a real network effect, speed may have a clear economic purpose. Research by Michael Katz and Karl Shapiro in 1985 explained the basic idea. A product may become more valuable to each user as more people use it. That can start a powerful cycle more.Users create more value. More value attracts more users. An early lead may then build into a lasting advantage. In these markets, even the product with the best technology does not always win. Starting late can become a growing problem.

Pete Flint of NFX argued in 2020 that companies with genuine network effects may have good reasons to choose growth before profit. Some markets can become winner take most races after reaching critical mass. A company may also have a chance to move from losses to profit. But there's a trap hidden inside the word growth. A rising customer count does not prove that a strong network is forming. NFX presents Groupon as a warning.Its vast expansion hid the loss.Of merchants and sellers that could not be sustained. The article also points to some direct to consumer companies in mattresses, shoes and meal kits. They used blitzscaling style growth without strong network effects or other clear defenses. Several later faced lower value funding rounds and investor losses. In other words, speed can build a fortress or simply make a weak business burn money faster.

NFX suggests annual growth of three to five times after product market fit at the seed or Series A stage. Later growth should work together with efficient customer acquisition. Useful checks include the Rule of 40 and recovering customer acquisition costs within about three to six months.
